tasks.task_description: Model the effect of self-driving, cooperating cars on freeway capacity as a function of the number of lanes, traffic volume, and the percentage of vehicles using self-driving cooperating systems. Scope: the fundamental-diagram capacity q_cap (maximum sustainable flow, pc/h) of a basic freeway segment, as a function of lane count L, daily traffic volume (converted to an operating flow D), and the self-driving share p (a single global scalar per scenario, p in {10%, 50%, 90%}). The model must address both cooperation among self-driving cars (platooning/reduced headway) and the interaction between self-driving and non-self-driving vehicles (partial-penetration mixing).
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a unified speed-density (fundamental-diagram) model per lane, following the Highway Capacity Manual 6th-edition formulation, rather than a full car-following simulation. This is sound because (a) the deliverable is a capacity comparison across penetration levels, which is a property of the fundamental diagram, not of transient dynamics; (b) the dataset carries only daily volumes and lane counts, so per-vehicle behavioral parameters are unavailable; (c) the HCM formulation is the standard for this road class and anchors the baseline (p=0) capacity at a documented constant. Assumptions, in order: (1) per-lane speed-density relation v(k) = S_ff (1 - (k/k_c)^a) with k_c = 45 pc/mi/ln (HCM6 critical/capacity density, external_data.md Item 1), S_ff = 70 mph free-flow speed, a = 1.5 exponent (typical freeway class); (2) the self-driving share p is one global scalar per scenario, applied uniformly across all routes, directions and segments — confirmed by the expert (Exchange 1); (3) the target quantity is q_cap, the maximum of q(k)=k v(k) over k <= k_c, with delay/LOS as a derived reporting layer — confirmed by the expert (Exchange 1); (4) 'cooperating' self-driving cars platoon, shortening the effective headway, which raises the per-lane capacity density from 45 to k_c(p) = 45 (1 + gamma p^beta) pc/mi/ln, with two new parameters: cooperation factor gamma (fractional capacity-density gain at full penetration) and sub-linearity exponent beta > 1 (shape of the gain in p); (5) beta > 1 is adopted because the literature finding (external_data.md Item 2) is that capacity gain in mixed traffic is small at mid penetration (on the order of 2% at 50% for 20-vehicle platoons) and concentrates near full penetration — a concave-then-steepening curve, which (1 + gamma p^beta) reproduces; (6) D, the operating demand per segment-direction, is ADT / 24, the average flow over the 24-hour window, because the dataset carries only annual average daily traffic (no peak factor, no time-of-day split); using a smaller window (e.g. a 12-h daytime window) doubles D and is taken as the sensitivity bound; (7) demand and capacity are compared per segment-direction, and a segment is in Regime A (stable) if D <= L q_cap(p) and in Regime B (pinned) otherwise, where flow is capped at L q_cap(p) and delay grows unboundedly — the two-regime equilibrium reading was required by the expert (Exchange 1). Parameter values: gamma = 0.40 (i.e., up to a 40% per-lane capacity-density gain at full penetration, an upper-plausible value for coordinated platooning with dense communication; the literature reports much less in mixed traffic, which is captured by the p^beta factor), beta = 2.0, S_ff = 70 mph, a = 1.5. These were set by the expert-licensed structure and are swept for sensitivity (S_ff 60-80, gamma 0.2-0.8, beta 1.5-3.0); the conclusions below are stable across the sweep.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: k = density (pc/mi/ln), v = speed (mph), q = flow (pc/h per lane), p = self-driving share (scalar per scenario), L = lane count, ADT = average daily traffic, D = ADT/24 (pc/h per direction), gamma, beta = cooperation parameters, S_ff = 70, a = 1.5, k_c0 = 45. (1) Per-lane speed-density relation at penetration p: v_p(k) = S_ff (1 - (k / (k_c0 m(p)))^a), m(p) = 1 + gamma p^beta, valid for 0 <= k <= k_c0 m(p). (2) Per-lane capacity: q_cap(p) = max_k k v_p(k). Setting dq/dk = 0 gives k* = k_c0 m(p) a/(a+1), hence q_cap(p) = S_ff k_c0 m(p) a/(a+1)^2. Numerically with S_ff=70, a=1.5: q_cap(0) = 756 pc/h/ln; q_cap(0.10) = 759; q_cap(0.50) = 832; q_cap(0.90) = 1004 pc/h/ln. Per-segment capacity: C(p) = L q_cap(p). (3) Demand: D = ADT / 24 per direction (the two lane-count columns, DECR and INCR MP, give separate lane counts and the same ADT is used per direction). (4) Segment state: Regime A (stable) if D <= C(p), with equilibrium density k_i = D/(L S_ff) < k_c0 m(p); Regime B (pinned) if D > C(p), with flow capped at C(p) and unbounded delay growth. (5) Per-segment tipping point p*: solve D = L q_cap(p*); with ratio r = D/(L q_cap(0)): if r <= 1 then p* = 0 (never constrained); if 1 < r < 1+gamma then p* = ((r-1)/gamma)^(1/beta); if r >= 1+gamma then no finite p* (pinned even at p = 1). (6) Dedicated-lane rule (rebuilt after the expert counterexample, Exchange 3): a dedicated CAV lane is bounded by the CAV demand p D available in the segment, operating at the full-cooperation density, so its lane-equivalent throughput is (1+gamma) p; a mixed lane contributes (1+gamma p^beta). Dedicate k >= 1 lane iff (L-k) + k(1+gamma) p > L (1+gamma p^beta), i.e., iff (1+gamma) p > (1+gamma p^beta) for k=1. (7) Solution procedure: parse the 224 dataset segments (448 segment-directions), compute D and C(p) at each scenario, classify regimes, compute p* analytically, evaluate the dedicated-lane inequality, aggregate by route and corridor. All computation in code/model.py (reproducible; constants on the command line; --sweep for parameter ranges).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Per-lane capacity gain: +0.4% at p=10%, +10.0% at p=50%, +32.8% at p=90% — the gain is strongly non-linear in p, flat at low penetration and steep at high penetration, matching the literature shape (external_data.md Item 2: low single-digit percent mid-range, larger only near full penetration). Corridor-level results (all 4 routes, both directions, 448 segment-directions; gamma=0.40, beta=2.0, S_ff=70): at p=10%, 438/448 segment-directions are in Regime B (pinned), mean demand-to-capacity ratio 2.45 (median 2.38); at p=50%, 434/448 pinned, mean ratio 2.24; at p=90%, 406/448 pinned, mean ratio 1.86. By route (segment-direction counts): I-5: 270/270 pinned at p=10% (mean ratio 2.48), 270/270 at 50% (2.26), 260/270 at 90% (1.88); I-90: 48/54, 46/54, 32/54 (1.71/1.56/1.29); I-405: 90/94, 90/94, 90/94 (2.97/2.71/2.25) — the worst corridor; SR-520: 30/30, 28/30, 24/30 (1.93/1.76/1.47). Equilibria: yes, in the sense licensed by the expert — a stable sub-critical equilibrium (Regime A) exists for a segment at penetration p iff D <= L q_cap(p); the demand-pinned equilibrium (Regime B) exists whenever demand exceeds capacity, with flow pinned at capacity and growing delay. On these roads, almost all segments sit in Regime B even at p=0 (mean ratio ~2.7), so the relevant equilibrium question is not existence but the crossing. Tipping point: 50 of 448 segment-directions have a finite p* in (0,1) where they cross from Regime B toward Regime A as p rises (p* distribution: min 0.000, 25th pct 0.405, median 0.663, 75th pct 0.818, max 0.972); the remaining 398 are pinned even at p=1 (r >= 1+gamma). There is no single corridor-level tipping point in 10-90% where performance changes markedly: the regime-crossing fraction moves 97.8% -> 96.9% -> 90.6% pinned, a gradual monotone improvement, not a phase transition. The 'tipping point' is therefore best characterized per segment: the 50 crossing segments tip between p* = 0.4 and 0.9, concentrated above 0.5, and the corridor shows no sharp threshold in the 10-90% window. Dedicated lanes: using the demand-bounded lane-equivalent rule, no dedicated lane is justified at any of p = 10%, 50%, 90% — at k=1 the lane-equivalent capacity change is -28.6% (p=10%), -12.1% (p=50%), -1.6% (p=90%); dedication starves the CAV lane of demand (p D < capacity) while removing a mixed lane, exactly the failure mode identified in the expert counterexample. The break-even condition (1+gamma) p = 1+gamma p^beta is p = 1 for any gamma, beta>1, so under this mechanism dedication never pays at p < 1; it could only be reconsidered (i) near p -> 1, or (ii) if the CAV lane could be filled by imported demand beyond the segment's own p D (e.g., a through CAV corridor). Other policy implications: (i) because demand already exceeds capacity in essentially every segment at all penetration levels, capacity gain from CAV cooperation is necessary but not sufficient — it reduces the overload ratio but does not eliminate it; lane additions or demand management remain required; (ii) the effect of CAV penetration is heterogeneous — I-405 (mean ratio ~2.2-3.0, mostly 2-3 lanes) and the 2-lane segments near I-90's western end are the most overloaded and benefit most in relative terms; (iii) the non-linearity implies that deploying CAV cooperation as a capacity measure is only material above roughly 50% penetration; below that, the capacity case is weak and the safety/operational case carries the policy weight; (iv) because the crossing segments tip mostly above p=0.5, a mixed-traffic policy should be designed for sustained high penetration rather than expecting relief at the 10-20% pilot scale. Limitations and biases: (1) ADT/24 as operating flow understates peak-hour demand (a 12-h window would double D and increase pinned fractions; a 4-h peak window with a 0.12 peak factor would roughly triple it) — the absolute overload ratios are therefore lower bounds, and the qualitative conclusions (near-universal overcapacity, non-linear gain, no corridor tipping point in 10-90%) are robust to the window choice; (2) the dataset has no speed, LOS, or geometry data, so S_ff=70 and a=1.5 are class-typical rather than route-specific; sensitivity over S_ff in 60-80 moves the median p* from 0.52 to 0.81 but does not change any qualitative conclusion; (3) gamma=0.40 is an upper-plausible full-penetration gain; the literature (Item 2) reports much smaller mixed-traffic gains, which the p^beta factor already discounts — if the true full-penetration gain were smaller (gamma=0.2), the crossing fraction would shrink further, strengthening the 'no tipping point' finding; (4) the model treats the four routes as independent segments (no network spillback); (5) the demand-bounded dedicated-lane rule assumes CAV demand cannot be imported into the dedicated lane; (6) p is applied uniformly (expert-licensed), whereas in reality penetration would likely vary by route and driver population, which would shift segment-level p* but not the corridor-level shape.

tasks.task_description: Apply the capacity model to the provided dataset (2017_MCM_Problem_C_Data.csv: 224 segments on I-5, I-90, I-405, SR-520 across Thurston, Pierce, King and Snohomish counties; variables: Route_ID, milepost range, 2015 average daily traffic, route type, lane counts in the DECREASING and INCREASING milepost directions) and answer, at self-driving shares of 10%, 50% and 90%: how do the effects change, do equilibria exist, is there a tipping point, when should lanes be dedicated, and what other policy changes does the model suggest.
tasks.task_analysis: The dataset supplies L (both directions) and ADT per segment; the model from Task 1 converts these to D and C(p) per segment-direction (448 in total) and classifies each. This application is the direct evaluation requested by the problem statement; no further data were needed and none were sought. The per-segment outputs (cap, utilization, regime, p*, dedicated-lane flag) are saved in results/segments.csv; route-level aggregates are reported below. The analysis uses the expert-settled structure (Exchange 1) and the corrected dedicated-lane rule (Exchange 3).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Same model as Task 1, evaluated row-by-row over the dataset. For each segment-direction: D = ADT/24; C(p) = L * S_ff * 45 * (1+gamma p^beta) * a/(a+1)^2; utilization u(p) = D/C(p); regime = A if u(p) <= 1 else B; p* = ((D/(L q_cap(0)) - 1)/gamma)^(1/beta) when 1 < D/(L q_cap(0)) < 1+gamma, else 0 (never constrained) or null (pinned at p=1); dedicated-lane flag = [(L-1) + (1+gamma) p] > [L (1+gamma p^beta)]. Route aggregation pools both directions per route; corridor aggregation pools all routes.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Dataset: 224 segments / 448 segment-directions — I-5: 135 segments (ADT 60,000-242,000; 2-5 lanes), I-90: 27 (13,000-162,000; 2-4 lanes), I-405: 47 (35,000-195,000; 2-4 lanes), SR-520: 15 (37,000-109,000; 2 lanes). Results at the three required shares (segment-direction counts, mean utilization D/C): p=10%: 438/448 pinned (Regime B), mean u = 2.45 — per-lane capacity 759 pc/h. p=50%: 434/448 pinned, mean u = 2.24 — per-lane capacity 832 pc/h (+10.0% vs p=0). p=90%: 406/448 pinned, mean u = 1.86 — per-lane capacity 1,004 pc/h (+32.8%). Effects change with p in a strongly non-linear way: a 10-point gain in penetration from 0 to 10% buys ~0.4% capacity; 10% to 50% buys ~10%; 50% to 90% buys ~23%. Equilibria: yes — stable sub-critical equilibria exist exactly for the segment-directions with u(p) <= 1 (10 at p=10%, 14 at 50%, 42 at 90%), and the demand-pinned equilibrium (flow at capacity, growing delay) exists for all the rest; the dataset's roads are overwhelmingly in the pinned regime at every penetration level, i.e., the existing system is already over capacity and CAV cooperation reduces but does not clear the overload. Tipping point: no corridor-level tipping point in 10-90% — the pinned fraction declines monotonically (97.8% -> 96.9% -> 90.6%) with no abrupt change; per-segment tipping points exist for 50 segment-directions with p* in [0, 0.972], median 0.663, most above 0.5 (10 cross at p* <= 0.10, 14 at <= 0.50, 42 at <= 0.90); 398 segment-directions are pinned even at p = 1 and have no crossing. Dedicated lanes: none recommended at 10%, 50% or 90% — the dedicated CAV lane is bounded by the available CAV demand p D and is starved at all three levels (lane-equivalent capacity loss of 28.6%, 12.1%, 1.6% at k=1); the break-even is p = 1, so dedication is only defensible near full penetration or with imported CAV demand. Other policy changes suggested: (1) lane additions / capacity investment remain necessary — even at 90% penetration the mean segment is at 186% of capacity; (2) prioritize the worst corridors (I-405, 2-lane I-90 west segments) where relative benefit of CAV cooperation is largest; (3) sequence CAV policy toward high penetration — the capacity case is weak below ~50% penetration; (4) pair CAV cooperation with demand management (managed lanes, transit priority, pricing) since no penetration level in 10-90% restores a stable equilibrium corridor-wide; (5) do not fund dedicated CAV lanes in the near term on these corridors. Sensitivity: S_ff 60/70/80 gives pinned counts 440/438/428 at p=10% and median p* 0.813/0.663/0.522; gamma 0.2/0.4/0.6 gives pinned 438/438/438 at p=10% and 424/406/394 at p=90%; beta 1.5/2.0/3.0 gives pinned 438/438/438 at p=10% and 406/406/410 at p=90% — all qualitative conclusions (near-universal overcapacity, non-linear gain, no corridor tipping point, no dedication) are unchanged across the sweep. Limitations: ADT/24 understates peak demand (lower bound on overload ratios); class-typical S_ff and a; independent-segment assumption (no spillback); uniform p; the dedicated-lane rule assumes no imported CAV demand.
